speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are just
one or two points I should like to emphasize. We have been told again and again that we should have a scientific tariff. It seems to me that is an absolute impossibility. I think we might as well give up the idea of having anything in the nature of what might be termed scientific in connection with our tariff. Undoubtedly all tariffs of which we have acknowledge have not been built up on any ground that could be properly designated as scientific. The fact is that as soon as we begin to talk about tariffs we get into politics, and I think we must all recognize that such financial adjustments are related to the economic life of the country, and so are and should be essentially political.
In introducing this bill the Prime Minister immediately carried us into the atmosphere of the court room. He suggested that the tariff commissioners should occupy the position of judges. That very presentation shows that he is not thinking in terms of the research laboratory but rather in legal terms, and of a situation in which the judge is supposed to adjudicate between two contending parties.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: To exercise judgment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Yes, to exercise
judgment between two contending parties, two contending forces or two contending ideas. I submit that this is altogether removed from the atmosphere of the scientific laboratory. In fact, conditions do not exist in connection with matters of this kind which permit of scientific treatment. We cannot possibly direct private business, under our present economic system, in accordance with the findings of such a commission. Our business people would not stand for it; those in this parliament who represent the big interests would not stand for it, so I think we might as well give up the idea that we are trying to establish a scientific tariff. I quite agree with what was said by the last speaker with regard to the impossibility of securing facts without having some theories by which to arrange those facts. I think that is admitted by all scientists. We must have some working hypothesis; otherwise the facts we collect are absolutely unrelated. As I face this vote my trouble is that the measure seems to be essentially a proposal designed to stabilize high protection; I think that is the danger. Almost all the provisions of the bill give that indication. I do not think we should do anything that will help entrench high protection.

Tariff Board-Mr. Woodsworth
I do not want to go into the general question of protective tariffs, but it does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time we are trying our level best to make trade follow or be confined within the political divisions -what has been recently termed "economic nationalism"-at the very time trade is transcending the narrower political bounds and is destined in the future more and more to act independently of those political boundaries. This simply means that a few interested parties, groups or corporations, are attempting to use governmental machinery to advance their own interests. The other day I heard of an American, who had a branch factoiy here, who asserted that he was the greatest British imperialist in Canada. I think that a very illuminating remark. I think it was quite true; those who come from the United States set up their businesses here and influence governments to make various tariff arrangements which will play into their hands. W e are deceived by the mere outward appearances and the appeals to patriotic motives which have no real basis in fact.
In introducing this bill the Prime Minister did enunciate a principle which is rather plausible; that is, that tariffs should be based on the equalization of production costs. If that were the real basis of protection I am not sure but that I could be induced to become a protectionist, because that might mean the protection of certain standards of living in this country. If that were a genuine proposal through and through I think there might be something said for protection, but that statement requires a good deal of examination. Emphasis is laid on the labour costs notwithstanding the fact that labour costs constitute only a percentage, and very often only a small percentage, of the entire cost. Further than that, there has been no guarantee in the past in any tariff legislation we have had that the standards of labour would be protected. There is one clause in the present bill, subsection (c) of section 4, which suggests possible action in that direction, but on the whole I do not think it can be said that labour is protected or likely to be protected because of high tariffs.
Indeed the danger is that the presentation by the Prime Minister tends to keep up the fiction that the tariff is guaranteeing high standards of living, which I do not think is the case. The other day the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond) made a very excellent speech. Unfortunately I could not follow him in the French language, but his remarks have been translated into English and I would direct the attention of hon.
members, especially English-speaking ones, to that speech. The hon. member for Beauharnois gave in some detail the history of the leading textile companies, and the dividends paid, and he said:
Nevertheless, dividends paid by textile companies in Canada have increased 11J per cent in 1928 as compared with the average dividend paid from 1922 to 1926.
The hon. member then gave the history of different textile companies, and in connection with the Dominion Textile Company he said:
The very first year, it paid on this common stock a dividend of $6 per share, or the equivalent of 60 per cent on this investment. The dividend was increased from year to year up to 1922, when it had reached $12 per share, which represented 120 per cent on the original investment.
And again:
From 1924 up to this date, the company has paid, without interruption, dividends which are equivalent to 150 per cent on the initial investment of $500,000, and 15 per cent on the second subscription of $2,500,000 made in 1922.
And so on with the other companies. I do not intend to take up time to give the details, but I would like to turn to the other side of the picture, to the conditions prevailing among the labour people employed in this industry. The hon. member said:
At present the worker employed in the Montreal Cottons Mills at Valleyfield receives less wages and works two or three times harder than previous to the increase in tariff. Moreover, machinery has replaced hand-labour, and while production is greater, less hands are employed.
And again:
Young girls who, in the spring of 1930, operated three warpers, machines which are used to prepare the thread to make cotton goods, were paid $30 every fortnight; now they operate six warpers and are paid less than $22.
In connection with weavers, he said:
With reference to the weavers, a worker who operated four looms and was paid $40 every fortnight, now operates six and is paid but $22 to $25 every fortnight-40 per cent less.
And so on in a number of other instances. I think it must be conceded that the tariff is not in any sense a guarantee of protection to the standard of living of the workers.
There is only one advantage which I see in tariff boards-whether like the old tariff board or the one now proposed-and that is the publicity which may come from the investigations of such a board. It does seem to me that in the present bill the publicity is being cut down considerably. One clause already has been objected to, and I take objection as well. This is what is known as the confidential

Tariff Board-Mr. Woodswcrrth
section, being subsection (10) of section 5, under which confidential evidence is not to be given to the public. I take the position taken by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young). The other day I stated my position when the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) refused to give the house certain information which he said was of a confidential nature. It seems to me that as soon as any business comes asking favours of the government, which in reality is the people, the people should know the conditions which prevail in that industry. That industry is no longer a private industry, the public has become a partner in it. The public has put a certain investment into that industry and the private owner or the corporation manager has no right under those circumstances to regard the conditions of that industry as being private.
During his first presidential campaign President Wilson said that in the old days the owner of a house adopted the English principle that an Englishman's house was his castle, and always contended that what went on in his house was his business. The president then referred to the great apartment buildings which were becoming common and to the fact that the owners were trying to apply the same doctrine to the great apartment blocks. He stated that in the old country they had adopted another principle and claimed that when thirty, forty, fifty or sixty families lived in a great apartment or tenement building, it was only by accident that they were living under one roof-that the individual apartment, not the block, was the unit. The authorities took the right to police the corridors in order to see that they were kept in a sanitary condition, that they were properly lighted and so on, and to all intents and purposes the corridors of the apartment block were considered as streets which the public had a right to enter and supervise. President Wilson contended that the same thing was taking place in big business; the old conception had been that business was private, but while that might have been the case when an individual managed his own business, when it became a corporation it ceased to be private in the old sense and the utmost publicity was desirable. Even twenty years ago he took the position that the corporations had forfeited the right to the secrecy which they had hitherto claimed, and that their operations should be made public. If that is true of corporations which are not seeking any special favours from the public, it is much truer of corporations which come

to the country asking for special tariff concessions, which in reality means that they are asking the public to give certain doles in order that they may carry on their business. Such doles should not be granted without all the facts being disclosed.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) reads as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that any tariff board entrusted with the duties set out in this bill, and more particularly with making inquiry into and reporting on matters pertaining to tariff and taxation, should at all times be such as to enjoy the confidence of the government of the day, and that accordingly the members of such board, unless appointed upon the recommendation of independent agencies representing different views or interests, should hold office only during pleasure.
That amendment recognizes that a tariff board is necessary in this country, and that the policy of this government should include the appointment of a properly constituted tariff board. Parliament which provides for the constitution of such a board has a right to dictate the regulations and conditions under which that board will function. This is not an amendment denying the necessity or expediency of having a tariff board in Canada; it recognizes the fact that a tariff board is essential. It however makes one qualification, namely, that the members of such board, unless appointed upon the recommendation of independent agencies, representing different views or interests, should hold office only during pleasure. It suggests the alternative of a tariff board, the members of which will be appointed on the recommendation of independent agencies representing different views or interests. Where in this country do those so-called independent agencies representing different views or interests exist? Is it to be, as suggested, according to the statute of Argentina, that this tariff board shall represent boards of trade or other political bodies scattered throughout the length and breadth of the land? I think not. I think the leader of the opposition and his party would be the first to oppose a tariff board which was appointed by the different boards of trade, by the different economic interests of this country. A board thus obtained, in view of its appointment and constitution could not properly function to carry out the purpose and intent of this legislation. Therefore I leave that element of the amendment out of consideration.

Tariff Board-Mr. Cahan
The object of the amendment is to secure the appointment of a tariff board which shall enjoy the confidence of the government of the country and hold office only during pleasure. If I understand that aright, it means that the amendment advocates the appointment of a partisan political committee which on all occasions shall act as the tariff board of this country.
* Mr. HANBURY: That is what the government is going to give us.

speechtext: That is the object and intent as expressed on the face of the amendment Which is now before the house. I cannot support an amendment of that kind and I shall state my reasons simply. I am no high tariff advocate, despite the gibes I sometimes receive from the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young). But the House of Commons in which this government has a majority has been elected on a certain tariff policy. I do not think it is a policy of high tariffs.

speechtext:
That is a matter of opinion and I am willing to discuss the question on almost any occasion as I have discussed it in the past. I think the essential purpose of the tariff is not to extend under all circumstances and conditions our purchases from foreign countries. If Canada is to be sustained as an independent nationality, developing from year to year and from century to century, it must in its present stage encourage the development of industry to the extent feasible for giving employment to the men, women and children of this Dominion. In so far as we deprive the people of Canada of employment for which they are suited, of employment in industry which is adapted to the conditions of this country and its northern climate, and facilitate the transfer of such employment to foreign countries, in just so far, in my opinion, is that policy antinational and prejudicial to the present and future development of our national life. The occasion, it seems to me, of the present commercial depression in Canada is that to too large an extent we have placed our wellbeing in the hands of and subject to the financial and commercial changes which take place in other countries over whose prosperity we have no control whatever. In so far as we make Canadian producers dependent at all times and under all conditions upon procuring abroad a market for their products, a market which is subject not only to financial depression but to every political whim and change of economic policy in those foreign countries,
in just so far are we giving hostages to fortune which this country cannot afford to give, and which we will not give if we adhere to a proper policy for our industrial and financial development.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: I do not wish to be interrupted. If I have finished my remarks within forty minutes, I shall be prepared to answer any questions. I am simply stating my position. I do not contend we should undertake in Canada any industry which we are not reasonably prepared to carry on and develop. I repudiate the idea that, as has been suggested in the house, we are advocating a protective policy which tends to prohibit all interchange as between Canada and other nations, but I take the view that the government and the party supporting it have been elected on a pledge and platform that in so far as tariffs may encourage industries which are suited to the conditions and climate of this country, in so far will such industries, if they may reasonably be maintained here, be maintained under the tariff policy of this government. I know hon. gentlemen opposite are opposed to that. I have heard on every platform throughout Canada the suggestion that foreign trade is more advantageous to us than domestic trade. Canada would disappear as a country of fairly well-to-do people if we were to become a free trade nation under all conditions, at the present stage of our development. Every industry in which we are now engaged would be practically wiped out or would be subject to financial disaster if we were to adopt such a policy. Protection must be the policy of this country.

speechtext:
I suggest to this house that the amendment is based on the idea that a partisan tariff policy is likely to be carried out under this bill which is now before the house, and I think I am quite as much in order, Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman who preceded me. It is necessary to create a board which will be a fact-finding board, which will consistently and independently investigate the facts and conditions of which knowledge is necessary in order to enable the government to determine what the application of its tariff policy shall be with respect to certain commodities or certain industries. Instead of relying upon such speeches as that of the hon. member for Beauhamois (Mr. Raymond) the other day, it is necessary that we should have a tariff board which may ascertain the facts upon which the textile tariff is to be based in order to give reasonable protection to labour and industry in this country, and yet so framed as to prevent profiteering, to which I am as much opposed as any hon. gentleman on the other side of the house. Therefore I say that we must have a board upon whose findings of fact the government and the house may rely in initiating and carrying into effect the tariff policies of this country.
There is no objection to saying that this party xs a protectionist party. Of course it is. This party and this government were elected on the policy of protecting home industries to every reasonable extent, in order to encourage those industries, in order to increase employment in this country, and in order to promote and advance the national industrial and commercial life of Canada. If our tariff policy does not attain those ends the people of this country will turn this party out of office.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Quite so, and what more do those hon. gentlemen opposite desire, who advocate entirely different policies? What more do they desire than that we should make errors in our fiscal policy? They will then publish those errors from one end of this country to the other. According to their idea, by passing this bill we are simply furnishing them with campaign propaganda for the next federal election. Well, we furnish it.

If we had not undertaken to carry into full effect our pledges and promises, despite the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite may differ from us in their opinion as to what those policies should be, they would be the first to rise in their seats, as member after member on the other side has already done, and accuse us of hypocrisy and deceit, and of not having the courage to carry into effect the policies which we placed before the country , at the last election. This government is going to cany out its pledges. It is prepared to stand or fall in this house or elsewhere upon a reasonable program of protection to the various industries of this country which is so framed as to prevent them from being driven to the wall either by sabotage of unfair competition or by the dumping of foreign products. Let gentlemen opposite accept the issue!
The government, in order to carry out its pledge, desires to be reliably informed by independent investigators with regard to essential facts. The hon. member for Hants-Kings is entirely in ei'ror, in so far as he suggests a subtle meaning to the terms of the proposed statute. This statute will not give an iota of authority to the tariff board to dictate or control the tariff policy of this country. I do not think that the tariff is such a partisan matter that it is impossible to obtain the services of members of a board who will be so free from party influences and who will appreciate to such an extent their high duties and their responsibility to this house and to the country, present and future, that they will make independent examinations and report the facts which must necessarily be ascertained in order to enable a government of either party to determine what increases or reductions should be made in the tariff. Therefore I am in favour of that board. So are hon. gentlemen opposite. But it must be a board of as independent a character and as independent in authority as it is possible for such a board to be. If this government proves incapable of appointing the proper personnel to that board, if the board functions hereafter as the partisan committee which hon. gentlemen opposite desire by this amendment, then this parliament will have ample cause seriously to object to the manner in which the board is functioning, and parliament must hold this government, and this party which supports this government, responsible therefor. But I have not so far lost faith in my fellow-countrymen as to believe that while we can procure competent men for appointment to high judicial positions, and men to accept appointments to high commissions

Tariff Board-Mr. Cahan
of state, we cannot find a sufficient number of men to fill the places on this board, who will act honestly and truthfully and conscientiously as a fact-finding commission. Such a board is necessary. I have listened to addresses in this house, in which alleged facts are assumed by members, reading from this or that document and drawing inferences from this or that statement. Such views, when expressed on either side of the house, are of no real value because those opinions are not based upon facts. I know something about the textile industry in my own province of Quebec.
Mr. ST-PERE:	I know something about

speechtext:
I do not believe there is
any country in the world to-day where the operatives in the textile industry were better protected and received a higher wage and enjoyed a better standard of living, than they did in the province of Quebec up until the time of the depression in this industry about a year ago. I examined into the conditions, and I found that what was driving people out of employment in the very district which my hon. friend represents was the fact that cheaper labour was being employed in certain branches of the textile industry in the United States, and elsewhere, where, in addition, there were no proper regulations as to the hours of employment or the employment of children. They were using that labour to dump into the province of Quebec, chiefly through the city of Montreal and the city of Quebec, textile products which came into competition with ours and drove our textile operatives out of employment by the hundred. Is it not possible to find some men in this country who are so competent, who are sufficiently nonpartisan and sufficiently independent in character, who have had such expert experience in economic matters, that their report on such competitive conditions would be of advantage to the government and parliament? That is the aim of this bill.
I am not going to discuss any more details in connection with it; I shall not express my views as to whether the members of the board should be eligible as candidates at federal election. I am not going to discuss now to what extent the board should be allowed to receive in confidence the information given on oath before it. Every hon. member who has had any connection with industry knows that no company with regard to certain facts relating to its industry would give the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, unless their evidence as to their own methods,
inventions and equipment were protected and treated as confidential. I am not going to make any observations concerning the question of patronage, as to whether or not the governor in council should appoint the, servants of the board. Those matters may be discussed subsequently. I shall not at this time state whether I think the commissioners should be appointed for ten or six years. They should be appointed for such a number of years however as would ensure the retaining of men of honest and conscientious minds, men with high qualifications who would leave their permanent employment to take positions on the board. They must be men who have had wide experience, and unless there is a certain stability to the term of their employment we will not be able to secure the services of such highly qualified men for service on the board. For those reasons I am not going to state whether they should be employed for a presidential term and a half, as is done in the United States. In that country, where the presidential term is only four years, they are appointed for six years. I am not going to say whether in Canada they should be appointed for seven or ten years, as compared with our parliamentary term of five years. I do not think, that such men of character, experience, judicial qualifications, and of scrupulous and conscientious conduct need necessarily fear that they would be, subject to the partisan influence of any government or of any political party.
This bill represents an earnest effort to take the ascertaining of facts with respect to industry in its relation to tariff out of the realm of mere political opinion and political controversy. If the new board is a failure the government must take the entire responsibility therefor, and it must take full responsibility for every specific tariff item which it brings before the house as the result of the investigations of the board.
I repudiate the idea that the board which will be constituted under the proposed statute will control the tariff of this country. Certainly it would not control my vote either as a member of the government or as a member of this house, and I am sure there are other hon. members of the government and hon. members in the house who will take exactly the same position. We are anxious however to ascertain the facts upon which proper and reasonable judgment may be based.
The amendment constitutes a vote of want of confidence in the government. While recognizing the necessity for a tariff board it recommends that such tariff board shall be

Tariff Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
a partisan committee of one political party, and nothing else. That is an amendment to which I am entirely opposed. I believe that as a government we must go on and carry into effect the tariff policy of this country. If we do not carry into effect the views which we expressed in the last election campaign, we are to be condemned. If we do not do so, we will prejudice the best interests of our people and preclude the development of our industrial life. If we fail the people of this country will withdraw their confidence from this government and elect my hon. friends opposite to carry out any policy which is suitable to their fancy.

Mr. Speaker, I believe
an explanation was given on the first reading of this bill, but I might say that it is a bill to grant eartain privileges to' certain promoters. I have been instructed to ask this house to send the bill before a committee for further consideration.

Mr. Speaker,
I rise to oppose the second reading of this bill, which is by no means as innocent as it looks. We have heard about wolves in sheep's clothing, and this is another instance. Ostensibly the bill is to incorporate The Soldiers' Aid Society. That sounds very beautiful, but if the bill is studied it will be found that the amount of money which will go to the soldier? will be but a small portion of that collected from the people of Canada. There might be no objection to clause 1, 2 and 3, but clause 4 gives an indication of the powers asked for. It reads as follows:
The society shall, under the provisions of this act, have power throughout Canada, subject to the approval of the attorney general of each province:
(a)	to promote the welfare of the Canadian veterans of the great war;
(b)	to print, establish, distribute and offer for sale lottery tickets, and grant prizes in cash to the winners thereof, notwithstanding any provision of the criminal code, chapter thirty-six of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, or any other statute of Canada, and, incidental and auxiliary thereto, to acquire property, printing presses and generally to engage in the printing business.
Section 7 reads as follows:
The net profits shall be distributed on the following basis; eighty-two per cent to be

distributed to the various veteran organizations in Canada, with the proviso that they shall take care of other veterans, who are not members of any organization. The remaining eighteen per cent shall be used by the society for administration purposes.
A short time ago a similar bill was before the other house and was defeated by a considerable majority. I think that house in so acting did itself credit and spoke the mind and will of the people of Canada. I am quite certain that when the true nature of this bill is brought to the attention of this house the support it will receive will be very meagre indeed.
I do not believe that the people of Canada have come to the position where it is necessary to depend upon the gambling instincts of the people in order to support the returned soldiers. We went into the war pledged to give the last man and the last dollar to the winning of the war. I am prepared as a member of this house to pledge all the resources of Canada in order that those who suffered and sacrificed in the great war may receive their just deserts, but I am not prepared to sacrifice the moral well being of the people of Canada for that purpose. I do not think the soldiers expect that that should be done.
I understand that the procedure in the case of a private bill is that on the second reading it is sent to the proper committee unless there is objection to the principle. I object strenuously to the principle of this bill and I oppose its second reading. I am satisfied that when the vote is taken this measure will be overwhelmingly defeated and we will hear nothing more about it.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny): Mr. Speaker, I am not opposed to the principle of this bill, but my character may not be of the high quality of that of the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Brown). I agree with him that we are not treating our soldiers fairly, and unfortunately many of them have to live upon public charity. In order to give relief to the returned men it may be necessary some day to introduce a bill of this character, but it should be introduced by the Canadian Legion or some similar body. I know for a fact that the returns received from the army and navy veterans' sweepstakes in Quebec have been supporting the families of many soldiers. I am not opposed to lotteries, because I do not think there is anything very immoral in risking a dollar, even though one may not receive a fair return for the gamble, if it is desired to call it a gamble. I do not suppose 22110-197
that the welfare of the country will be endangered by any lottery of that description, but this bill contains a radically vicious principle. As long- as our criminal code remains as it is and is not amended, lotteries are prohibited, with only two exceptions, the Art Union of London, England, and the Art Union of Ireland, and I am certainly opposed to a private bill being introduced to permit something that is prohibited by the criminal code. This bill is introduced with the intention of giving to a certain class of citizens of this country, a so-called soldiers' aid society, the power to do what is prohibited by the criminal code. They are proceeding in the wrong way. The first thing to do would be to amend the criminal code and then to ask for the passage of a bill of this nature. Therefore, until the criminal code is amended in this regtard, I deem it my duty to oppose this bill on principle on the second reading.

I take somewhat the same stand as that taken by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), although from a rather different angle. I have no particular objection to lotteries or raffles, except that I never win anything at them- possibly that is the source of my objection'- but I rather disagree with the hon. member for Lisgar when he says he thinks he speaks the mind and will of the people. I believe at the present moment it would be popular to pass an act legitimatizing lotteries; that is the mind of the people of Canada at the present day. There are various reasons; they have burned their fingers in the stock market, land booms and oil booms, and now, with the proverbial propensity of people to gamble, they are proposing to gamble in this way. A number of winning tickets have been taken recently in Canada in some of the big world sweepstakes, and that has turned the public mind in that direction. That does not necessarily mean that because this is popular for the moment we should do what in our judgment is not in the best interest of the country. That is the way I look at the matter. I do not believe it would be to the ultimate benefit of the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Lisgar has referred to the bill which was defeated in the upper house. It was confined to lotteries on behalf of hospitals, and I think almost every hospital in British Columbia telegraphed or wrote to the members representing that province in support of that bill, possibly because they saw an immediate means of relieving them of what is very often a distressful task, that of raising money. Had that bill come to the House of Commons, I should have opposed it because

Private Bills

I do not think it would have been ultimately a success. If you are going to allow this sort of thing for a hospital or, in this case, for what is at least alleged to foe for the benefit of soldiers, you have to allow it for other purposes equally worthy. If you do not do so, the law will be ignored anyway, because there will be a sort of moral justification for doing so. That leads you on a little further until you have lotteries galore, when every little village, will be getting up a lottery for some purpose, all more or less worthy. I do not like the way in which this bill is drafted. It says it is to promote the welfare of Canadian veterans of the great war. That of course is desirable, but not by way of a lottery. As the hon. member for Lisgar says, I do not think we, have to come down to that in order to promote their welfare. Then clause 7 provides:
The net profits shall be distributed on the following basis; 82 per cent to be distributed to the various veteran organizations in Canada, with the proviso that they shall take care of other veterans, who are not members of any organization.
That seems rather a peculiar provision to insert. They are not compelled to take care of their own veterans, but they must take care of other veterans who are not members of their own organization. That is rather unhappily worded.
Unlimited lotteries would lead to abuses we do not now foresee, and I have under my hand a couple of instances which illustrate this. A day or two ago a daily paper carried a column under the heading "Lottery swindle nipped in the bud by United States police". To put it shortly, in Boston they had a scheme by which they were going to rob the people of Canada and Mexico to the extent of $2,500,000 a week. They had a fake Irish Free State sweepstate; they had printed forged tickets and they were getting ready to sell them at the rate of that value a week. The article says that the man proposed to issue 1,000,000 tickets weekly; the first batch of tickets selling at $2.50 each had been distributed already. How many people would have been absolutely stung because no prizes were going to be distributed at all? A great deal more of that sort of thing would take place and that would lead ultimately to people turning away in disgust against the whole principle of these things. They would find so much illegal action going on they would discount the whole thing, and the hospitals, which by that time would be dependent upon that source, would be left in the lurch.
I have another instance which I might give. Before I left home, in the backwoods of
[Mr. Neiil.)
British Columbia, someone brought me a book of sweepstake tickets that had been sent to him to sell. It was some sweepstake in Quebec and he asked me to find out about it. It appeared to be all right, but he was a little doubtful. I made fairly diligent inquiry among Quebec members, lawyers and so forth and not one of them had heard of that lottery. It was being sold in remote places, being apparently another instance of the kind which was discovered in Boston.
I am not opposing this from a religious point of view, but I do not think it is good policy for the people of Canada to embark on it. As we have the object lesson of the upper chamber turning down another similar bill, limited I think to one province, I do not believe it would be wise on our part to go ahead at this late stage of the session and pass this bill to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
It should not be necessary for me to have to say anything in support of this bill. As we are all aware, the Bank Act as it stands, by subsection 1 of section 91, limits to 7 per cent the rate of interest which a bank may charge on loans. This may be the practice of the banks in central Canada and in the far eastern parts of this country, but in most of western Canada, on

Bank Act
account of the fact that there is no penalty clause, this provision of the Bank Act has been very largely ignored and rates of eight and sometimes nine per cent, and even as high as ten per cent have been charged. Needless to say, no business, and particularly that of agriculture, can possibly continue with such a high rate of interest being charged, and for that reason I have introduced this bill calling for a penalty to be inserted for violation of the provisions of section 91, penalizing either the bank or its officials if the law is broken in the future.
To give a few figures to show how this provision of the Bank Act is being ignored, I may say that 134 places in Alberta were canvassed, and at 105 of these places 8 per cent was being charged. At every other place, with one exception where less than 8 per cent was being charged, the rate was higher than 8 per cent, and in some cases ran as high as 10 per cent. The same story is true with regard to Saskatchewan. Of 79 places that were canvassed, 8 per cent was being charged at 53 places, and in all the others-with one exception, where 7 per cent was called for- a higher rate than 8 per cent was called for. It is quite unnecessary for me to point out how unfair it is for the banks of this country to charge these exorbitant rates of interest contrary to the law as defined in the Bank Act.
I might add that no sooner had I placed my bill on the order paper than I received considerable correspondence from all over Canada, supporting the bill which is now before the house. I shall not bother the house with reading them all, but I should like to quote from one which I think is well worth reading because it comes from a board of trade and is so wholeheartedly in favour of the bill which is now before us. It comes from the Indian Head Board of Trade, and reads:
At a meeting of our board held yesterday, a hearty endorsation of your move to have the limitation of bank interest enforced at 7 per cent was fully approved by all members.
I was instructed to write you and congratulate you on bringing down a bill of such far-reaching importance particularly to the west.
We wish you every success in this matter, and sincerely trust you will be able to make it effective.	_
We are quite sure it will meet with the entire approval and support of everyone in the west.
Yours sincerely,
Guy Watson,
Secretary, Board of Trade.
With these few words, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the house to give this bill very sympathetic consideration and support.

speechtext:
It should not be necessary for any member of this house to say anything in support of * measure of this kind. Its purpose is simply to make effective the original intention of parliament with respect to that clause in the-Bank Act which limits the maximum rate of interest which may be charged to seven per cent. There is no doubt in the world that parliament intended that the banks should not be permitted, under any consideration, to charge a higher rate of interest than seven per cent, but by taking advantage of technicalities the banks have been deliberately ignoring that clause of the act and have been charging in western Canada rates as high as eight and ten per cent. I know there is a common argument-I have read it many times in the press since this bill was introduced into the house-that if one places any restriction on the banks, it will curtail the amount of money available for loans, and that therefore the very people who are supposed to be helped will automatically be injured. That is an old, old argument. It was used years ago against the factory acts in England, and against practically every other reform since. I will say frankly that if a farmer cannot secure money as cheap as seven per cent, he had better not borrow at all. The bank would be doing him a kindness to refuse him a loan at a higher rate of interest. But in most cases the money is borrowed at eight per cent. That is the case in my constituency to a large extent. When a farmer who has borrowed money from a bank happens to have a bad crop and cannot pay off his indebtedness, his note is renewed at as high a rate as 10 per cent. There are many farmers in my constituency who have second mortgages on their farms to-day, which were given to the banks to secure a bank loan which the farmer was unable to meet, and these mortgages bear a rate of 10 per cent. In ordinary times, or even when business is buoyant and prices of farm commodities are reasonably high, no farmer can possibly pay off loans at such a rate as that, and at the present time, with conditions as they are, it simply means that any little equity the farmer may have in his chattels and land is absorbed. We may as well recognize and face this issue. I think in the end it will be a good thing for the banks themselves to have this provision enforced because I believe the fact that they have been permitted to charge these high rates of interest in western Canada has induced them to take chances which they should not take. They have loaned money to people to whom they should not have
Bank Act

loaned it, and for purposes for which bank money should not be loaned. It seems to me that the only effect this bill would have would be to make the banks more careful to make sure when they do loan money that the risk is a good one and that the money is to be used for proper purposes.
Of course, we shall be told that a farmer or a business man should not borrow money at these rates. But the banks are in control of the funds, and very often a farmer or business man finds at a particular time that he cannot get along without a loan, and when the money is available there is a temptation to borrow more than one really needs. But if the banks were restricted to charging a maximum of seven per cent, they would not have the margin they now have to play on at high rates of interest, and they would be very much more careful in making loans. So I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the passing of thi3 bill, thereby carrying out the original intention of parliament in this regard, would be a good thing for the banks themselves.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot support this bill, because I must confess that the extremity of its provisions shocks my sense of proportion. I am indeed very sympathetic with what has been said by hon. members from western Canada in regard to farmers being charged excessive rates of interest for loans, but the Bank Act already contains a provision which puts a limitation on the rate which may be charged upon such loans. By this bill I contend that its sponsor proposes to take away from the field of civil law the provision which is now in the Bank Act as a safeguard against the exaction of exorbitant rates of interest. If the bank commits a breach of that provision of the act, the bill makes that breach a criminal offence, and not merely a criminal offence, but a very serious criminal offence, because the bill provides that it shall be an indictable offence, and the penalties prescribed are indeed heavy.

Now, I hope my hon. friend will not rise and tell me that that is exactly what the banks are doing, only that they are acting with a little more finesse. If my hon. friend was going to make that suggestion, I am pleased to say that I am ahead of him.
May I ask hon. members to go back for a moment to the inherent right of individuals, and in a moment I shall deal with the rights of corporations. I think we may all agree that inherently every individual has the right to make a bargain or a contract with any other individual as a matter of business relations. True, in the public interest parliament finds it necessary from time to time to interfere with that inherent right or freedom of bargaining. Parliament exercised that right in the case of those people who were exacting usurious interest, and to prevent a recurrence the Interest Act was passed by this dominion parliament. Unless however some great social wrong or injustice is being done I am unable to appreciate where there is any justification in this parliament or any other legislative body placing restrictions upon ordinary business contracts and relationships, although I confess there is a tremendous tendency in modern times so to do.

Because parliament confers upon a corporation such as a bank which, in its final analysis is a creature of the statute of parliament, certain rights and privileges, we say to that corporation, "If you are to exercise these rights and privileges we will restrict to some extent your operations". With that in view we say we have the right to restrict the amount of interest which shall be charged. The statute

Bank Act
already provides that an amount of interest in excess of 7 per cent is not recoverable and cannot be recovered by a bank through the judgment of any court of law. I am not so much opposed if the sponsor of this bill thinks it might be advantageous to those whom he desires to benefit, to have the word "recoverable" changed to "charged", but for the life of me I cannot see any justification in legislating against one particular class of corporation, merely because that corporation is engaged in a certain class of business. To my mind it is not fair to constitute, as a criminal offence any action taken by a bank which would not be criminal if taken by any other corporation or by an individual. To my mind such legislation is the rankest kind of discrimination. The sooner we get away from discriminatory and paternal legislation in our parliament the better it will be for the business of Canada.
Now I am ready for any questions my hon. friends may wish to ask.

speechtext: I had not intended at this time to speak in the house on this matter. But let me say that although the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Lawson) is on the same side of the house as I am, I disagree with him absolutely and fundamentally. I think, Mr. Speaker, that there are occasions when onerous contracts are entered into which certainly ought if possible to be prevented by parliament. I know in the constituency I represent the rate of interest is far too high, and if conditions continue as they are the interest will never be recovered. I was amazed at the illuminating information which was presented to the house by the hon. member who sponsored the bill. May I say at this point that I support the bill and I hope it will pass the house. I believe if it does pass it will be real and substantial evidence that we realize the situation in which the western farmer is placed at the present time. The gentleman who headed the firm in the city of Winnipeg with which I was articled as a law student said that he did not believe there ever was a dollar made that was worth more than 7 per cent interest-. I agree heartily with that gentleman's statement. To my mind, in view of the decrease in the price of commodities a reduction in the rate of interest to 6 per cent would be quite in keeping. For these reasons I heartily support the bill.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
I agree with some of the statements made in support of the bill, and also with some of the remarks
of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson). I do not like the penal clauses in the bill. subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: That is already in the act.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: If the bill receives second reading it should receive it only on condition that the committee to which the bill is referred shall have the privilege of recommending changes along the line I have suggested, or along some other line.

speechtext:

Hon. RAYMOND D. MORAND (East Essex):	One must sympathize with the
sponsor of the bill when the fact is realized that the maximum rate of interest has been stipulated by statute. To my mind however the chief trouble does not lie in the rate of interest charged because the contract wherein the interest charge appears is made between the man borrowing and the man lending. There should be and I think there is a big difference between the rate originally charged and the rate charged when a loan is renewed. When the bank takes advantage of the fact that the man is unable to pay his loan and tries to charge a higher rate of interest than is covered by the contract, and he not being able to borrow the money from other quarters is forced to renew his loan at a higher rate, I certainly think the bank is at fault and I have a great deal of sympathy for the borrower. I believe if the sponsors of the bill had made some change whereby the rate of renewal should not exceed the primary rate, which after all is 7 per cent in the Bank Act, they would accomplish the purpose they have in view and it would not be necessary to include in the bill such severe penalties.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE

so far as I am concerned. On all the notes I have ever signed-and I have signed a good many-the rate of interest was always stated; in many cases it was printed on the face of the note. I should feel much more inclined to support the bill if it were a question of renewal instead of the original loan.

speechtext: Let the bill go to the banking and commerce committee.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the present is a dangerous time to interfere with our banking institutions. They may be good, or they may be bad, nevertheless when the time of stress comes we all have to resort more or less to the banks to help us through.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext:

times; perhaps to-day they are not so good. But if at the present time Canada is financially sound, I for one feel that we may thank our banking institutions for that very desirable condition. I cannot see why we should now seek to amend an act which has been in force for so many years. True, 9 per cent may be too high a rate of interest. I never lived in the
Yukon. I think it would be well to defer consideration of this matter for a year or two. We all know that the banks are passing through a crisis, just the same as the rest of us are. The banks may have charged too high a rate of interest in some cases, but we in our turn may have charged more than was proper in connection with some of our transactions. For my part I cannot see my way clear to support the bill at the present time.
(Mr. Morand.)

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: Mr Speaker, it does seem to me a startling proposition to attempt to make a purely civil transaction an indictable offence.

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: PROPOSED PENALTY FOR VIOLATION OF PROVISION RESPECTING INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
I have no doubt that the sponsor of this bill is influenced by the very best of motives and feels that conditions in his part of the country justify him in proposing legislation of this character. But to say that if on a private contract, purely legal on its face, a bank goes beyond a certain well-defined limitation-which in itself is not a high rate of interest-it should be guilty of an indictable offence and liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $5,000 seems to me hard to justify. But the penalty does not stop there. The section continues:
-and everyone who, being a director, manager or officer of any hank, violates the said provisions shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable, on conviction, to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.
That certainly is very radical and drastic legislation, and of a class and character which I do not think any member of this house after giving the matter his calm judgment would care to see put upon the statute books of this country. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he withdraw the bill in view of the fact that the Bank Act will in the ordinary course of events be revised in the next two years. If I recall correctly, he was a member of the banking and commerce committee when the Bank Act was last revised, and. at that time matters germane to the subject matter of this bill were under discussion. A change was made in the provisions of the act whereby it was provided that no matter what rate might ibe charged .on the face of a bill or a contract anything exceeding 7 per cent would not be recoverable in any action. I think the conditions have not materially changed since the banking and commerce committee refused to go as far as he desired, and that therefore the necessity for this bill does not exist. I can well sympathize with anyone who is desirous of legislating against usury, but I do not consider that any case of a usurious nature has been made out. There may be exceptional cases which the hon. gentleman seeks to deal with, but he should not predicate general legislation of this character upon isolated instances, and I think he would be well advised to withdraw the bill.

speechtext:
Speaking for myself,
I fully approve of the reduction in the vote for the air mail service at the present time. I believe that it is necessary and wise to keep up an air mail service in our wide northern spaces where no other means of communication exist, and where but for this service the people would be completely isolated. I doubt very much, however, the wisdom or the necessity in these times of financial stress of duplicating a perfectly satisfactory train service such as we have, for example, between Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto, or Winnipeg, Calgary and Edmonton. It is not a popular thing to say, but I have said it in other places, and I repeat it here. I fully approve of such a move on the part of the government. The air mail service is, as a matter of fact, of very little advantage where it is duplicating a fast train service. For example, I received a letter to-day that was sent me from Red Deer. It came by air mail and it took exactly to an hour the same length of time that it would have taken had it been sent by train, and so it has been with other letters that I have received by air mail from the west. There is no great saving of time, and in any case it does seem to me that we can find better uses for our federal money than in duplicating a train service that has always been found satisfactory. In some of these places served by the air mail there are fast trains running three and four and five and six times a day, and surely any business that has to be carried on between these places can be carried on by the train service. I very much approve of this reduction and I am glad to have the opportunity of stating here, as I have stated in the country, that the air mail service is totally unnecessary. It is a species of thrill that we can well afford to do without except in those wide spaces in our northern country, in Quebec, Ontario and the west, where for safety, convenience, and absolute necessity in some cases, an air mail service should be given. I am very glad to see that for the time at least, until we can afford it, this somewhat spectacular but absolutely unnecessary thrill is being cut off from our expenditure.

Rather, they should be continued, and we should vote whatever extra amount is necessary to keep them up. When the time comes I think I shall be able to prove by figures that the air mail routes in Canada charging only a two-cent rate have had a surplus over expenditures. To-day with the added one cent that surplus will be increased by $120,000. With the added rate the surplus will be in the vicinity of $350,000 or $400,000. While I am on this subject may I suggest to the government that if they add the one cent to the five cent air mail rate within a year the whole air mail service of Canada will be selfsustaining.
At the proper time I shall go into the figures more thoroughly. In view of the fact that I was the one who initiated the mail service, and in view of the fact that I took great pains to follow it up and tried to administer it properly the government may see fit to take a few hints from my remarks.

When this item was under discussion the other evening the minister spoke at great length about immigration into this country from Europe having ceased. I should like to ask if he has taken any steps to stop immigration from the orient.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I think the hon. member could not have heard me aright when we were on this item previously. Immigration from Great Britain has not stopped and has not been restricted. The only difference is that we are not now, as was the case in the past, encouraging movements of people from Great Britain. Any Britisher who wants to come to Canada-I think I used the term before, under his own steam-without relying on Canada to coax him here and pamper him after he gets here, is as welcome as anyone else. I 'hope the time will never come when there is any restriction against people coming to this country from Great Britain.
With respect to immigrants from the continent of Europe, very rigid restrictions have been placed against the movement of those people to Canada, not because any one of the races has not very desirable people but because it is the policy of this government to exclude them until we take care of the difficulties through which we are now passing.
With respect to oriental immigration, as I presume the hon. member knows, that is governed entirely by the Chinese Immigration Act and the agreement, sometimes called a treaty, with Japan. So far as I am aware, the Chinese Immigration Act is being religiously adhered to. There are and will continue to be some few who may evade the preventive force and get into this country, but the departmental officials are alive to the necessity of strictly enforcing that law, and of course it is the policy of this government to see that it is enforced.

Our investigating officers from time to time find some Japanese who have entered the country illegally. They are deported. I think I am not exaggerating when I say there is an average of eight or ten per month who we find have come to Canada in defiance of that agreement. Of course the hon. member very well knows, coming from that locality, the difficulties which have arisen from time to time with those coming into Canada from the orient, but so far as I am aware the preventive officers of the department are endeavouring to see that both the Chinese Immigration Act and the agreement with Japan are adhered to.
