speechtext: I am rather surprised to hear the hon. member state that he has personal knowledge of a number of Japanese who have illegally entered this country, because the records in my department do not disclose any information coming from him. When information is imparted to the department to the effect that people have entered illegally, an investigation is made just as promptly as the officers can undertake it, and if the hon. member or anyone else will send to the department information such as he indicates he possesses, an investigation will be held.
The newspaper article states that the immigration authorities are checking up on this matter, and I should like to know if the minister has received their report.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have not seen the press
despatch to which the hon. member has referred. The department cannot rely upon such despatches in order to institute investigations. These investigations in connection with the illegal entry of people from the orient are going on all the time, and if the hon. member has any information which would assist the department we should be glad to have it, because it might prove helpful in the conduct of such investigations.
Will the minister make an inquiry regarding this press despatch?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Another despatch I have quotes Hon. N. Lougheed, Minister of Lands in the provincial government, as saying:
As it is well known that many orientals do not register, the figures are probably below the mark.
The same despatch contains the following:
Check-up of orientals attending public schools in the province showed that while the white school population had increased only five per cent since 1927, the Japanese attendance had jumped 38 per cent. Chinese increased only three per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
think the situation is quite as bad as my hon. friend would have it. In times gone by the immigration officials were more or less ignorant of the so-called gentleman's agreement which existed at that time. That agreement was not in the form of a treaty, but was more or less of a vague understanding. A Japanese would come along and ask admittance under that agreement, and he would be allowed to enter without any further investigation. There was a great deal of slackness, and the Japanese came in in excess of the number permitted under the agreement. It was left largely to the honour of the other party to the agreement, and I am sorry to say that that honour was somewhat lacking. In one year as many as 1,800 have come in, whereas the agreement ostensibly confined them to 450. Along about 1925 the late government revised this gentleman's agreement and to a large extent eliminated its provisions. It was stipulated that the future immigration of Japanese would come under the same regulations as those applying to other aliens, and that they would toe subject to the same investigation, restriction and scrutiny. One exception was made in that 75 men and 75 women and children were permitted to enter each year. At that time I took a great deal of trouble to see whether or not the system was operating. I was given some opportunity to observe the methods used and I was convinced that the Immigration department was living up to the desire of the government to put every restriction upon Japanese coming into this country. When a Japanese or Chinese comes along and says he is a merchant, they do not just take his word for it; he is followed up and when it is found there is anything fraudulent in his statements, he is promptly sat upon. I remember one particular instance in connection with Chinese where they had a fake merchant business in Montreal, of all places. A man would apply for entry and certify that he was a partner in this company and had put in so much money. The immigration officers would go down to Montreal and would see this man hard at work in this company in which he was supposed to have put $500 or $2,500, I forget which. The department became sus-

Supply-Immigration

picious, and upon going back a few months later they found that this man had gone, taking his money with him, and another man had taken his place. Regulations were enacted which stopped that practice, and any man coming in as a merchant is subject to close scrutiny.
The minister said that he thought Japanese were being deported at the rate of six, seven or eight per month, but I think he will find that those men who are being sent back came in during the ^lack period I have mentioned. Every once in a while a Japanese gets the urge to visit his native country, but before obtaining a passport or a ticket entitling him to return again, he has to reveal when he came in and upon what boat. If it is found that he came in illegally, he is shipped out of the country and not allowed to return. There was a regular system in vogue to bring these Japanese into the country. They were wanted to work in the canneries up at Skeena or elsewhere in the north, but it was necessary that they be British subjects. They had a bunch of about twenty-four Japs who could speak a little English; they were dressed decently and were more or less familiar with our system. A fraudulent notary public was employed and those men were naturalized over and over again, and the certificates were sent lip to the Japanese at the canneries, who had never seen the notary public or the judge, and who had been in the country perhaps only six weeks. That sort of thing has been done away with. I think the feeling to which the hon. member for New Westminster is giving voice is what might be termed a carryover from the conditions which existed previously.
There is another factor to be considered, the enormous increase of the Japanese population in British Columbia. More trouble is caused by the stork than by the immigrant ship. These people have large families, and I think their birth rate is 38 as compared with 18 for the white man. It is that large increase which is going to cause us trouble in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: How can you stop that?

There are methods if the
minister has the courage to adopt them. I leave that to him. The other day I think I saw that in Steveston there was a 14-room school, in 11 rooms of which the pupils were all Japanese; in two they were mixed and in one they were white. That gives an idea of how the Japanese population is increasing. The Japanese question in British Columbia is like that of the negroes in the United States; we 
have them and we must put up with them. That is the general trend of feeling in British Columbia against the orientals. I think the committee will agree I have not hesitated in the past to attack the government for slackness in carrying out the regulations, but 60 far as I know, the regulations are being pretty strictly adhered to now.

After the census is taken, if
the registration of orientals shows there are more than the official records indicate, would the minister be prepared to investigate illegal entries into British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The investigation is going on constantly, and if in the census anything is disclosed that would seem to indicate there has been a defiance of the law, the investigation will be speeded up and pursued with vigour to determine the cause, and to deport any of those that we may find have come in illegally.

Having had the honour on more than one occasion to be in charge of the Immigration department, I have been much interested in this discussion I was somewhat perturbed the other night in connection with the exchanges between the minister and the hon. member for Bow River. I had visions of the day when I sat on the other side, when British Columbia members were bombarding me in regard to Chinese and Japanese immigration, and when I was forced on many occasions to take refuge by making somewhat rash promises that I found difficult to carry out because of international complications. When I heard the minister say the other night that he was going practically to shut off immigration, I began to wonder what was going to happen to men like the hon. member for Vancouver Centre behind me, the hon. member for New Westminster, the hon. member for Vegreville, the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Red Deer; and I was greatly disturbed. I rose simply to say how pleased 1 am to hear the minister state that there will be no restriction on gentlemen of that kind entering Canada even at the present time, because I wish to assure the minister the house would be in a serious plight if we did not have these hon. gentlemen in it. I was congratulating myself that I had been in control of the department when men of the calibre of those hon. gentlemen could enter. I want to assure the minister that I am heartily in support of allowing free immigration from the British Isles, and I hope it will be continued. We do get some obstreperous people from certain quarters, but,

Supply-Immigration
after all, it is a pretty good class of immigrant and I am greatly pleased they are not to be kept out.

As regards the question of
orientals, I forgot to make one comment to the minister, and I hope he will pay some attention to this. Under the gentleman's agreement, or what is left of it, the Japanese are allowed in, as I said, not to exceed 150 a year. As regards the Chinese the situation is practically exclusion. This is the point: when- this government came to power they very wisely passed an order in council prohibiting all immigration to our shores, but they did not make it apply to the Japanese. I think that was a mistake. The order in council was so worded that it did not apply to those who came in under treaty or other agreement. It might be put forward that the Japanese, an arrangement having been made, if not by a treaty, by an agreement, were not to be subject to this order in council. But after all the agreement was they were to be subject to the Immigration Act in every respect and if it were found necessary, under changed conditions, to prohibit all immigration, including English, Irish and Scotch, surely the Japanese themselves could not object if the same restrictions were applied to the agreement with them. They have a sense of fair play or at least of what it is wise to do, and I do not think they would have insisted on the letter of the agreement, for that is all it is, and on coming in despite the order in council. The result is that the white man is prohibited from coming here and yet he sees a certain number of orientals entering. That galls the British Columbian greatly. I am sure if the minister understood the situation, he would have no difficulty in dealing with it. The Japanese should be subject to any change in our Immigration Act; they are the same in that regard as everybody else.

While the enthusiasm of the ex-Minister of the Interior is perhaps justified so far as his remarks referred to hon. members in this corner of the house, yet for his information and in order that we may not become too enthusiastic about any immigration to this country, it would be well if the minister gave the committee the total number of deportations during each of the last two years of British-born or foreign-born, that is, those not born in the British isles.

While the minister is looking that up, perhaps I might ask a question. I understood him to say there were no restrictions on British immigration to 22110-1881
Canada. Will a British immigrant not be under an obligation to prove that he has work or some subsistence here ahead of him?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Of course he is, and I think those in G-reat Britain who are engaged in the immigration of people to Canada are thoroughly aware that it is futile to send to this country to-day people who have nothing to live on for a reasonable period.
Just at this juncture I want to correct the impression that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni may unwittingly have made. I do not think he would create the impression by design-that white men are excluded from Canada and yellow men are allowed in. That is not a fair statement. There is no exclusion of people from England, Ireland and Scotland. I claim a fair degree of courage myself, but I do not think I am courageous enough to try to stop a Scotchman if he wants to enter Canada; if he wanted to get in he would get in. There is no exclusion, and the British people are aware of that fact. There is a section of the British press that does not seem to appreciate it, but the officials in Great Britain, with whom we are constantly in touch, are well aware that in the regulations there is nothing that places restrictions upon British people entering Canada. The only thing we have done is to stop, in so far as we can do so, assisting with money grants and things of that kind, people coming even from Great Britain. It may be that those grants will be renewed in the future, although for my own part, with my short experience in this department, I am satisfied that it is better to go slowly and let people come to Canada of their own volition, not assisted by some charitable organization whose members are impelled perhaps by quite laudable motives from their point of view to aid people to come to Canada from Great Britain but who do not know the type of settler likely to make good in this country and who do not know Canadian conditions. Such methods only give rise to disappointment and discouragement to these newcomers, and in the last eighteen months the records are very plain. Many hundreds of British people have been sent home, and I think I am not exaggerating when I say that much more than 50 per cent of these people have asked to be sent home. I could give many illustrations, although I do not want to dwell upon this for fear I may be misinterpreted. I do not want to create the impression that we in Canada have not the highest regard for the British people and British migrants who come here, but unfortunately it is true that a great percentage of those who have been returned1 to Great
Supply-Immigration

Britain have been returned because they wanted to go back. I know of my own personal knowledge down in the office in the Jackson building last fall, that young chaps of from eighteen to twenty-two and twenty-three would come in who I felt certain could get ahead in this country, but for one reason or another they wanted to go back. In the case of the younger ones I think it was homesickness more than anything else. I remember one morning a dozen came in. They deliberately went down to the mission and got some charity and some meals and got themselves reported. I interviewed them and pointed out that if they had a little patience and probably a little more courage than they seemed to exhibit they would get along all right in Canada, and we offered them work on the farms. They told me very frankly that they wanted to go home, that they did not want to go on the farm in Canada, and some of them were homesick. I pointed out to them, when they wanted to be returned home, that Great Britain was carrying a heavy burden, that they had been sent to Canada largely at the expense of the British treasury, and that they should try to buck up. But no; we had to arrange for the deportation of them all. The unfortunate part of it, from my own personal standpoint, was that some of them who went back under circumstances such as I am detailing were met at the boat by reporters, and when I saw some of the press despatches from the old country with respect to these people I thought there was no possible hope of my escaping criticism. I made up my mind, however, to do the best I could under the circumstances, and not read the newspapers. And that is what I have done.

If I have misrepresented my hon. friend's action I am very sorry. But it certainly was stated very prominently in the papers at that time, indeed it was almost heralded, that one of the first actions of the present government was to stop immigration. Am I to understand that that applied only to assisted schemes of immigration?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It applied to assisted schemes of immigration.
Only to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No, it went further than that, but not so far as to stop immigration. We stopped-I do not want to be extravagant in my language-misrepresenting the conditions in Canada to the British people, and we did not encourage people to come here when they would be disappointed in the conditions they would meet when they arrived. Our labour market could not absorb them. That is

as far as we went. If they wanted to come they could come. I think the government adopted a proper course in notifying them, not that they were not welcome here, but that conditions were such that they probably would have great difficulty in getting employment. That is as far as we went.
It is gratifying to hear the minister tell us that he stopped misrepresenting things. He was referring to the previous government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have not said that.

The minister said that he
thought it wise to stop misrepresenting things.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There are other people besides the late government who were interested in getting immigrants.

Oh yes, we are well aware of them. This order in council must have been in fairly precise language. It was not a question of giving instructions to agents to ease off, but an order in council was passed, I understand, to stop all immigration. What did that order in council say?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I probably can remember the effect of it.
What is the date of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have not before me the dates of the orders in council, but I think I can remember the effect of the order in council. Under order in council P.C. 183 the following people were allowed into Canada:
(1)	A bona fide agriculturist-
I do not know why they use the term "bona fide."
Mr. BF.AUBIEN: What is the date of that order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
April 8, 1926. The classes
allowed in were as follows:
(1)	A bona fide agriculturist entering Canada to farm and has sufficient means to begin farming in Canada.
(2)	A bona fide farm labourer entering Canada to follow that occupation and has reasonable assurance of employment.
(3)	A female domestic servant entering Canada to follow that occupation and has reasonable assurance of employment.
(4)	The wife or child under 18 years of age of any person legally admitted to and resident in Canada, who is in a position to receive and care for his dependents.
(5)	Any United States citizen entering Canada from the United States who shall satisfy the immigration officer in charge at the port of entry that he has sufficient means to maintain himself until employment is secured.
(6)	Any British subject entering Canada directly or indirectly from Great Britain or Ireland, Newfoundland, the United States of

Supply-Immigration
America. New Zealand, Australia or the Union of South Africa, who shall satisfy the immigration officer in charge at the port of entry that he has sufficient means to maintain himself until employment is secured:
Provided, that the only persons admissible under the authority of this clause are British subjects by reason of birth or naturalization in Great Britain or Ireland, Newfoundland, New Zealand, Australia or the Union of South Africa.
(7)	A person who has satisfied the minister that his labour or service is required in Canada.
(8)	The father or mother, the unmarried son or daughter, eighteen years of age or over, the unmarried brother or sister, of any person legally admitted to and resident in Canada, who has satisfied the minister of his willingness and ability to receive and care for such relative;
Provided, that this clause shall not apply to the relative of any resident in Canada who himself failed to observe the conditions under which he was admitted to Canada.
That is the old order in council. If my recollection serves me aright-I speak subject to correction-in the new regulation class (1) is allowed in, but it is changed to read:
(1) An agriculturist entering Canada,
And so forth.
What is the date of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
August 14, 1930. I think this was changed not in the regulations itself, but was changed by a departmental circular to our agents in the various countries. The effect of the new regulation was that we admitted an agriculturist entering Canada to farm if he had sufficient money or funds to engage and continue in the business of farming. No specific sum was mentioned, but our officers were circularized in every instance and advised that they would be charged with the responsibility of inquiring into the background of each migrant coming to Canada to see that he knew something of agriculture, and that we were not admitting people from the cities who would be hopeless in an effort to run a farm. Personally I do not know anything about farming, but I am told, and I believe it to be true, that it requires a great deal of skill and considerable experience to run a farm properly, just now anyway.
The regulations with respect to class 2, dealing with farm labourers, and class 3, dealing with female domestic servants, were repealed. Class 4 was allowed to remain; that is the wife or child under eighteen years of age of any person legally admitted to and resident in Canada, who is in a position to receive and care for his dependents. It was obvious that if a man has migrated to this country, had established himself and wanted to bring his wife and infant children here, he
should be allowed to do so, but in every case where an application is made by a man, from whatever country he may come, to bring his wife and children into Canada, I have given instructions, and I believe that they are being religiously adhered to, to inquire into what that man is doing and, if he is in industrial employment, to see whether or not his employment is likely to continue. If he is on a farm, investigations are made. At times it is difficult to be too restrictive with respect to such immigration, but I confess I am checking up with a degree of severity so that we shall not add to our present economic difficulties. The regulations with respect to the United States and Great Britain remain unchanged, with the exception that a subsequent order in council with respect to the United States excluded the people coming to Canada from that country who were not citizens of it. Before the order in council was put through many people could come in from the United States whose status in that countiy was such that if they became public charges in Canada we could not deport them back to the United States. Those people therefore were restricted by a subsequent order in council.

What about the nationality
of the classes to which you wrere referring? Did they have to be British, or could they be alien?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: From the United States?

No, the farm labourers and
the domestic servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The labourers and the
domestic servants are excluded, with the exception of the United States and Great Britain.
That applies only to European aliens?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Yes. Then the seventh
clause was repealed,-
A person who has satisfied the minister that his labour or service is required in Canada.
Rightly or wrongly I felt that that class would give me a great deal of anxiety, if I had the right to supersede the regulations by my own say-so. I am told that regulation No. 7 was the clause that gave rise to what was known as the permit system. I am not going to deal at length with that system, but to my mind it was probably as great a mistake as could have been made. I am told that at election .times, members are importuned by certain of their electors with regard to the issuance of permits to bring in relatives and friends, and that embarrassment results to the member if the requests are not complied with.
Supply-Immigration

Has that been
absolutely done away with.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes. Since I have been at the head of the department I have signed one permit, and that is all. It was a meritorious case, that of a student coming to one of our universities.

Can the minister tell us if
Japanese coming from Hawaii enter Canada as citizens of the United States or citizens of Japan? Great numbers come from Japan to Hawaii, from Hawaii to the United States and from the United States to British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am told there are no
Japanese coming from the Hawaiian islands; they must come from Japan. I do not know where the hon. member got his information.

Quite a few thousand came
into British Columbia at one time from Hawaii. In one year 5,000 came in from the Hawaiian islands.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
That was about 1907 or
1608?
Probably so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The first agreement was
entered into because of the large number that were coming in. Under the first agreement from 400 to 500 came in yearly. Then in 1928 the agreement was revised by the late government and the number was cut down to about 150 a year. That is the agreement under which we are operating at present.
Are there any Japanese coming from Hawaii now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am instructed no
Japanese have come from Hawaii for many years.

My information is that they
are given papers in the United States and come right through to British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There have been no complaints to the department since I have been in charge. I shall inquire, however.
Very well. I shall be satisfied if the minister looks into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
If the condition described
by the hon. member exists, it will be properly investigated.

I desire to enter
a protest against the attitude of some of the hon. members towards orientals. I do not want unrestricted immigration by any means. I do not think however that we help our international problems by maintaining an at-

titude such as that which has been evidenced to-night by some hon. members from British Columbia. We must remember that the oriental nations are great nations on the other side of the Pacific ocean with which we hope to develop trade relations. If we are too harsh in such matters there is a possibility of provoking a feeling of resentment on their part. I hope we will not deal too vigilantly with the people who happen to live in the oriental countries.
I wish particularly to refer to the nonencouragement of immigrants from Great Britain. The minister has made no statement concerning juvenile immigrants. I wish to invite his attention to a question passed as an order for return which appeared on the order paper under my name, and which has not yet been answered. On page 2966 of Hansard of June 24, I find the question:
Is the British Immigration and Colonization Association now operating under the administration of the Department of Immigration?
And the further question:
Is the policy to bring more British boys to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I think I can answer my
hon. friend's questions. Last fall I received information from premiers of the different provinces as to how many boys those provinces could absorb. The province of Ontario asked for 200. Saskatchewan at first asked for 60, but I pointed out that I thought it desirable to cut the number down to 40. At the present time I am not sure whether they have received 38 or 40. The western provinces, with the exception of Saskatchewan, did not think that they should have any boys this year, so none came. Quebec took the same stand; New Brunswick wanted 150 and Nova Scotia 75 boys.

What societies
brought these boys in?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In Saskatchewan the government and the Church of England; in Ontario the Catholic Immigration Society, the Y.M.C.A. and some other religious and charitable organizations joined with the Ontario government to take care of 200 boys. As to the maritimes, I am not at present seized of the facts. But the movement of boys has been restricted to the desires of the provinces. I thought that was a fairly safe method to adopt this year.

Is the British
Immigration and Colonization Association operating under the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have not the papers
before me to go fully into the history of

Privilege-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
the association, but it was started about eight years ago with a view to bringing boys from Great Britain to Canada. At first their funds came mainly from British sources and were supplemented by some voluntary subscriptions by people in Canada. Later the railway companies, the British Empire Settlement board and the Canadian government contributed to the expenses of bringing the boys here and for their after care on arrival. The association operated under a dominion charter. About a year ago it fell on rather difficult times, in fact I am instructed that from its inception there was apparently a lack of business capacity on the part of the board of directors. At any rate, the money subscribed from the sources I have indicated was exhausted earlier than it should have been, with the result that late last year the company found itself in financial difficulties, and under obligation to a number of boys whom they were to look after for a certain time after their arrival in Canada. Confronted with that position last October and November, in conjunction with the heads of the department who look after colonization, I had an interview with the railway companies-they had contributed considerably more than we had to the association's funds- and we came to the conclusion that we would have practically to take over the work. We accepted the resignation of the directors, and in order to save the expense of setting up a new organization, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways supplied a certain number of the staff from their own colonization departments, and my department supplied a man who is very well qualified to carry on work of this character. That is the method we are now employing in carrying on the institution.

You have to
assume all responsibility for the boys?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: We have to.

In the case of
fares that have been advanced do the government collect from the boys?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No, the fare is a gift from the British Empire Settlement board.
Does the minister mean to say that the advances are being collected, or are not being collected?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: They are not being collected, and of course no more boys have been brought out since last year.
If fares have been advanced, the government is not now collecting them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No. I am told that at
no time have advances been made to juveniles.

Then if no fares
are being taken back from the boys, some of them are being deceived, and certain persons are collecting fares when they ought not to be doing so. It is a matter for very serious investigation.
Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman, I want to ascertain the facts with regard to this matter.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, June 29, 1931.
